items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "continuous variation"?
options: Variation that results in a limited number of distinct phenotypes with no intermediates, for example ABO blood group.
Variation that results in a range of phenotypes between two extremes, for example height.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA.
items.answer: Variation that results in a range of phenotypes between two extremes, for example height.
items.markingKey: Continuous variation: variation that results in a range of phenotypes between two extremes, for example height.

items.stem: Explain why height in humans shows continuous variation.
items.answer: Height is controlled by many genes and also influenced by the environment (diet, health), so there is a range of values between two extremes.
items.markingKey: many genes [1]; environment [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a gene mutation can result in a different phenotype.
items.answer: A change in the base sequence changes the sequence of amino acids, so the protein made has a different shape and may not work (or work differently).
items.markingKey: base sequence changed [1]; amino acid sequence changed [1]; protein shape / function changed [1] [3]

items.stem: A student in Singapore collects data on flower colour in snapdragons and height from her class. For each feature, state the type of variation and the type of graph she should draw.
items.answer: Flower colour in snapdragons: discontinuous, bar chart; height: continuous, histogram.
items.markingKey: discontinuous + bar chart [1]; continuous + histogram [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Lima collects data on seed shape in peas (round or wrinkled) and leaf length from her class. For each feature, state the type of variation and the type of graph she should draw.
items.answer: Seed shape in peas (round or wrinkled): discontinuous, bar chart; leaf length: continuous, histogram.
items.markingKey: discontinuous + bar chart [1]; continuous + histogram [1] [2]

items.stem: A group of students in Hanoi grew sunflower plants from seeds of the same variety. Half were grown in fertile soil in full sun and half in poor soil in shade. The heights of all plants were measured after six weeks. (a) Explain why plants grown from the same variety still showed a range of heights within each group. (b) Suggest why the plants in fertile soil and full sun were taller on average.
items.answer: (a) Genetic differences between seeds (alleles from sexual reproduction) and small differences in local environment. (b) More light and minerals (e.g. nitrate for protein) give more photosynthesis and growth; environment affects phenotype.
items.markingKey: (a) genetic variation [1]; environmental variation [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which type of variation is usually caused by genes only?
items.answer: Discontinuous variation
items.markingKey: Discontinuous variation (e.g. blood group) is caused by genes alone.

items.stem: Explain why identical twins raised apart can have different body masses.
items.answer: They have identical genes, so differences must be caused by the environment, such as diet and exercise.
items.markingKey: same genes [1]; environment [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar measured the foot length of 8 students in Cairo: 26.4, 23.6, 23.0, 25.8, 26.0, 22.4, 24.6, 27.9 cm. (a) Calculate the mean foot length. (b) Calculate the range. (c) State the type of variation shown.
items.answer: (a) 24.96 cm (b) 5.5 cm (c) continuous

items.stem: Yusuf measured the height of 10 students in Riyadh: 177, 154, 159, 175, 150, 168, 150, 169, 155, 168 cm. (a) Calculate the mean height. (b) Calculate the range. (c) State the type of variation shown.
items.answer: (a) 162.5 cm (b) 27 cm (c) continuous

items.stem: A group of students in Cairo grew maize plants from seeds of the same variety. Half were grown in fertile soil in full sun and half in poor soil in shade. The heights of all plants were measured after six weeks. (a) Explain why plants grown from the same variety still showed a range of heights within each group. (b) Name one feature of these plants likely to show discontinuous variation and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Genetic differences between seeds (alleles from sexual reproduction) and small differences in local environment. (b) Flower colour (or seed colour): controlled by one or a few genes, giving distinct categories.
items.markingKey: (a) genetic variation [1]; environmental variation [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "cuticle"?
options: A plant adapted to live in water or in very wet conditions.
A plant adapted to live in dry conditions.
An inherited feature that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment.
The waxy, waterproof layer covering the epidermis of a leaf.
items.answer: The waxy, waterproof layer covering the epidermis of a leaf.
items.markingKey: Cuticle: the waxy, waterproof layer covering the epidermis of a leaf.

items.stem: Explain how sunken stomata reduce water loss in a xerophyte.
items.answer: Humid air is trapped in the pit, so the concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the air is reduced, slowing diffusion.
items.markingKey: humid air trapped [1]; smaller gradient / slower diffusion [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a cactus can carry out photosynthesis even though its leaves are spines.
items.answer: Its green stem contains chloroplasts and carries out photosynthesis.

items.stem: A plant has large air spaces in stems and leaves. In which habitat is it most likely to live, and why?
options: Water (hydrophyte): this feature reduces water loss by evaporation
Dry habitat (xerophyte): this feature reduces water loss by evaporation
Water (hydrophyte): this feature keeps leaves afloat and allows oxygen to reach roots
Dry habitat (xerophyte): this feature keeps leaves afloat and allows oxygen to reach roots
items.answer: Water (hydrophyte): this feature keeps leaves afloat and allows oxygen to reach roots
items.markingKey: Large air spaces in stems and leaves → hydrophyte: keeps leaves afloat and allows oxygen to reach roots.

items.stem: A botanist in Dhaka describes two plants. Plant P has hairs on the leaf surface. Plant Q has leaves reduced to spines. For each plant, suggest whether it is a xerophyte or a hydrophyte and explain how the feature is adaptive.
items.answer: P: xerophyte — traps a layer of moist air, reducing transpiration. Q: xerophyte — gives a smaller surface area for transpiration.
items.markingKey: P xerophyte [1] + explanation [1]; Q xerophyte [1] + explanation [1] [4]

items.stem: Tariq measured the percentage loss in mass of shoots of four plant species, each standing in a test-tube of water covered with oil, over 24 hours in the same conditions. Results table. Plant species: sunflower, water lily, marram grass, oleander. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 9.3, 12, 1.6, 2.4; trial 2: 9.3, 11.5, 1.6, 2.3; trial 3: 5.5, 11.8, 1.6, 2.3. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it.
items.answer: (a) Temperature; light intensity. (b) Trial 3 for sunflower (5.5 %); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated).
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: temperature; light intensity; humidity / air movement; time; initial mass or leaf area of the shoot [2] (b) trial 3 for sunflower identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why hydrophytes have large air spaces in their stems.
items.answer: Air spaces keep the plant buoyant so leaves float near light, and allow oxygen to diffuse to the submerged roots.
items.markingKey: buoyancy / light [1]; oxygen to roots [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the fennec fox is adapted to living in hot deserts.
items.answer: Large ears have a large surface area with many blood vessels to lose heat; pale fur reflects heat / camouflage; kidneys produce concentrated urine to save water.
items.markingKey: any two adaptations with explanations [2] [3]

items.stem: A student counted stomata in a field of view of area 0.1 mm² on leaves of water lily and of a bean plant (a mesophyte). Water lily: upper surface 66, lower surface 1. Bean: upper surface 9, lower surface 35. (a) Calculate the number of stomata per mm² on the lower surface of the water lily. (b) Calculate the total stomata per mm² (both surfaces) for each plant. (c) Suggest how the distribution of stomata in water lily is an adaptation to its habitat.
items.answer: (a) 10 per mm² (b) water lily 670; bean 440 per mm² (c) stomata mainly on the upper surface, in contact with the air, for gas exchange; the lower surface touches water.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10 [1] (b) 670 [1]; 440 [1] (c) hydrophyte adaptation explained [2] [5]

items.stem: Ana measured the percentage loss in mass of shoots of four plant species, each standing in a test-tube of water covered with oil, over 24 hours in the same conditions. Results table. Plant species: bean, sunflower, marram grass, water lily. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 7.8, 9.1, 1.6, 7.1; trial 2: 8.3, 9.4, 1.6, 12.2; trial 3: 8.2, 9.5, 1.6, 12.3. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (c) State the type of graph that should be drawn to display these results and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Independent: plant species; dependent: percentage loss in mass. (b) Use percentage change in mass so shoots of different starting masses can be compared. (c) A bar chart, because the independent variable (plant species) is categoric.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = plant species [1]; dependent variable = percentage loss in mass [1] [2] (b) Any one from: use percentage change in mass so shoots of different starting masses can be compared; measure the leaf surface area and express the loss per cm²; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the plant species (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (c) bar chart [1]; categoric variable [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "antibiotic resistance"?
options: The ability of bacteria to survive treatment with an antibiotic that would normally kill them.
An environmental factor, such as a predator or an antibiotic, that affects which individuals survive and reproduce.
A strain of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria that is resistant to many antibiotics.
The process by which individuals with better adapted features are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
items.answer: The ability of bacteria to survive treatment with an antibiotic that would normally kill them.
items.markingKey: Antibiotic resistance: the ability of bacteria to survive treatment with an antibiotic that would normally kill them.

items.stem: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.
items.answer: A random mutation gives one bacterium resistance; when the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria die; the resistant bacterium survives and reproduces rapidly by binary fission, passing on the allele, so the population becomes resistant.
items.markingKey: mutation [1]; non-resistant killed [1]; resistant survive and reproduce [1]; pass on allele [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why it is important for patients to finish a course of antibiotics.
items.answer: Stopping early may leave the most resistant bacteria alive; these reproduce, increasing the proportion of resistant bacteria.

items.stem: A single resistant bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Assuming all survive, how many bacteria will there be after 3 hours?

A patient in Seoul had 100 000 bacteria in an infected wound. 95% were killed by an antibiotic; the survivors were resistant. (a) Calculate the number of bacteria that survived. (b) The survivors divide every 40 minutes. Calculate the number of resistant bacteria after 4 hours. (c) Explain why the antibiotic will no longer be effective.
items.answer: (a) 5 000 (b) 320 000 (c) all the bacteria now carry the resistance allele, inherited from the survivors.
items.markingKey: (a) 100 000 × 0.05 = 5 000 [1] (b) 6 generations [1]; 5 000 × 2^6 = 320 000 [1] (c) offspring inherit resistance [1] [4]

items.stem: A patient in Lagos had 50 000 bacteria in an infected wound. 99% were killed by an antibiotic; the survivors were resistant. (a) Calculate the number of bacteria that survived. (b) The survivors divide every 30 minutes. Calculate the number of resistant bacteria after 5 hours. (c) Explain why the antibiotic will no longer be effective.
items.answer: (a) 500 (b) 512 000 (c) all the bacteria now carry the resistance allele, inherited from the survivors.
items.markingKey: (a) 50 000 × 0.01 = 500 [1] (b) 10 generations [1]; 500 × 2^10 = 512 000 [1] (c) offspring inherit resistance [1] [4]

items.stem: Mateo placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria, incubated it at 25 °C for 2 days and measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Results table. Concentration of antibiotic / µg/cm³: 0, 2, 4, 8, 16. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 6, 8, 10, 13, 15; trial 2: 6, 9, 10, 12, 14; trial 3: 6, 9, 10, 7, 14. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Trial 3 at 8 µg/cm³ (7 mm); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) A line graph: concentration of antibiotic on the x-axis and mean diameter of clear zone on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 3 at 8 µg/cm³ identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; concentration of antibiotic on x-axis and diameter of clear zone on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria, incubated it at 25 °C for 2 days and measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Results table. Concentration of antibiotic / µg/cm³: 0, 5, 10, 20, 40. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 6, 12, 14, 17, 18; trial 2: 6, 17, 15, 16, 18; trial 3: 6, 12, 15, 17, 18. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Calculate the mean diameter of clear zone at 5 µg/cm³, ignoring any anomalous result. (c) State why the plates were incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C.
items.answer: (a) Volume of antibiotic solution on each disc; size of paper disc. (b) 12 mm (c) To reduce the risk of growing human pathogens.
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: volume of antibiotic solution on each disc; size of paper disc; type of bacteria; incubation temperature; time of incubation [2] (b) (12 + 12) ÷ 2 [1] = 12 mm [1] [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "an environmental factor, such as a predator or an antibiotic, that affects which individuals survive and reproduce"?
items.answer: Selection pressure
items.markingKey: Selection pressure: an environmental factor, such as a predator or an antibiotic, that affects which individuals survive and reproduce.

items.stem: What is the original source of the allele for antibiotic resistance in bacteria?
options: The antibiotic causes the bacteria to change
items.answer: A random mutation
items.markingKey: Resistance arises by chance mutation, before exposure to the antibiotic.

items.stem: A single resistant bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Assuming all survive, how many bacteria will there be after 3 hours?

In a study near Dubai, scientists released 134 dark and 100 pale peppered moths in a polluted wood where tree bark was blackened by soot. After a week they recaptured 37 dark and 14 pale moths. (a) Calculate the percentage of each type recaptured. (b) Explain the difference using the theory of natural selection. (c) Suggest what happened to the proportion of dark moths after clean-air laws reduced soot.
items.answer: (a) dark 27.6%, pale 14% (b) Dark moths were camouflaged on dark bark, so fewer were eaten by birds; they survived to reproduce and passed on the allele for dark colour. (c) It decreased, because pale moths were better camouflaged on clean bark.
items.markingKey: (a) 37 ÷ 134 × 100 = 27.6% [1]; 14 ÷ 100 × 100 = 14% [1] (b) camouflage / predation [1]; survive and reproduce [1]; pass on allele [1] (c) decreased with reason [1] [6]

items.stem: In a study near Toronto, scientists released 127 dark and 149 pale peppered moths in a polluted wood where tree bark was blackened by soot. After a week they recaptured 39 dark and 13 pale moths. (a) Calculate the percentage of each type recaptured. (b) Explain the difference using the theory of natural selection. (c) Suggest what happened to the proportion of dark moths after clean-air laws reduced soot.
items.answer: (a) dark 30.7%, pale 8.7% (b) Dark moths were camouflaged on dark bark, so fewer were eaten by birds; they survived to reproduce and passed on the allele for dark colour. (c) It decreased, because pale moths were better camouflaged on clean bark.
items.markingKey: (a) 39 ÷ 127 × 100 = 30.7% [1]; 13 ÷ 149 × 100 = 8.7% [1] (b) camouflage / predation [1]; survive and reproduce [1]; pass on allele [1] (c) decreased with reason [1] [6]

items.stem: Diego placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria, incubated it at 25 °C for 2 days and measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Results table. Concentration of antibiotic / µg/cm³: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 6, 14, 16, 17, 17; trial 2: 3, 13, 16, 17, 18; trial 3: 6, 14, 16, 17, 18. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Calculate the mean diameter of clear zone at 0 µg/cm³, ignoring any anomalous result. (c) Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: (a) Trial 2 at 0 µg/cm³ (3 mm); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) 6 mm (c) As the concentration of antibiotic increases, the diameter of clear zone increases and then levels off at about 30 µg/cm³.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 2 at 0 µg/cm³ identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) (6 + 6) ÷ 2 [1] = 6 mm [1] [2] (c) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "inbreeding"?
options: Another name for selective breeding, in which humans rather than the environment select which individuals breed.
An inherited feature that allows a crop or animal to resist infection by a pathogen.
Breeding closely related individuals, which reduces genetic variation.
The process of humans choosing individuals with desirable features to breed together, repeated over many generations.
items.answer: Breeding closely related individuals, which reduces genetic variation.
items.markingKey: Inbreeding: breeding closely related individuals, which reduces genetic variation.

items.stem: Describe how a farmer could selectively breed cattle that produce more milk.
items.answer: Select the cows with the highest milk yield and a bull from a high-yielding mother; breed them; select the best offspring and breed them; repeat over many generations.
items.markingKey: select parents [1]; breed [1]; select offspring [1]; repeat over many generations [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why selective breeding is faster than natural selection.
items.answer: Humans choose the parents directly every generation, so only individuals with desired features breed.

items.stem: Breeders in Cairo selected sheep with the most wool for 6 generations. The mean wool yield rose from 3.6 to 5.5 kg per year. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean increase per generation. (c) Describe the procedure the breeders used.
items.answer: (a) 52.8% (b) 0.32 kg per year per generation (c) selected individuals with the highest wool yield, bred them, selected the best offspring and repeated each generation.

items.stem: Breeders in Dubai selected sheep with the most wool for 10 generations. The mean wool yield rose from 3.2 to 4.1 kg per year. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Calculate the mean increase per generation. (c) Describe the procedure the breeders used.
items.answer: (a) 28.1% (b) 0.09 kg per year per generation (c) selected individuals with the highest wool yield, bred them, selected the best offspring and repeated each generation.

items.stem: Over 50 years, breeders in Doha have produced varieties of sheep with much greater wool yield than wild types. Some of these varieties are now very similar to each other genetically. (a) Explain one disadvantage of the varieties being genetically similar. (b) State two differences between selective breeding and natural selection.
items.answer: (a) Reduced genetic variation means a new disease or environmental change could affect all of them; alleles for resistance may have been lost. (b) Humans choose vs environment; features useful to humans vs features aiding survival; faster vs slower.

items.stem: Explain why genetic variation is reduced by selective breeding.
items.answer: Only a few individuals with similar alleles are bred, so other alleles are lost from the population.

items.stem: Explain why a crop variety that has been selectively bred for high yield may still be grown with fertilisers.
items.answer: The phenotype depends on the environment as well as genes; minerals are needed for maximum growth.

items.stem: In Istanbul, a farmer in a region with frequent droughts plans to breed maize. Suggest one feature to select for, and describe how selective breeding could be used to obtain it.
items.answer: Drought tolerance: choose parents showing drought tolerance, breed them, select offspring with the most drought tolerance and breed them; repeat for many generations.
items.markingKey: suitable feature [1]; select parents [1]; breed and select offspring [1]; repeat over generations [1] [4]

items.stem: Over 50 years, breeders in Bangkok have produced varieties of rice with much greater grain yield than wild types. Some of these varieties are now very similar to each other genetically. (a) Describe how selective breeding could have produced varieties of rice with greater grain yield. (b) Explain one disadvantage of the varieties being genetically similar.
items.answer: (a) Select plants with the most grain; breed them; choose offspring with the greatest grain yield; repeat over many generations. (b) Reduced genetic variation means a new disease or environmental change could affect all of them; alleles for resistance may have been lost.

items.stem: Which graph should be drawn to display data showing continuous variation?
items.answer: Histogram
items.markingKey: Continuous data are grouped into classes and drawn as a histogram with touching bars.

items.stem: Explain why discontinuous variation is shown as a bar chart rather than a histogram.
items.answer: The data fall into distinct categories with no intermediates, so bars are separate.

items.stem: The hand spans of 45 students at a school in Muscat were grouped into classes: 15.0–16.9 cm: 5; 17.0–18.9 cm: 9; 19.0–20.9 cm: 15; 21.0–22.9 cm: 13; 23.0–24.9 cm: 3. (a) State the modal class. (b) Calculate the percentage of students in the class 15.0–16.9 cm. (c) Explain whether this shows continuous or discontinuous variation.
items.answer: (a) 19.0–20.9 cm (b) 11.1% (c) continuous: a range of values between two extremes (data had to be grouped).

items.stem: Freya measured the height of 8 students in Auckland: 166, 162, 157, 152, 167, 167, 181, 175 cm. (a) Calculate the mean height. (b) Calculate the range. (c) State the type of variation shown.
items.answer: (a) 165.9 cm (b) 29 cm (c) continuous

items.stem: A group of students in Mumbai grew sunflower plants from seeds of the same variety. Half were grown in fertile soil in full sun and half in poor soil in shade. The heights of all plants were measured after six weeks. (a) Explain why plants grown from the same variety still showed a range of heights within each group. (b) Explain how a mutation could produce a new flower colour in this species.
items.answer: (a) Genetic differences between seeds (alleles from sexual reproduction) and small differences in local environment. (b) A random change in the base sequence of the gene changes the amino acid sequence of the pigment enzyme, so a different pigment is made.
items.markingKey: (a) genetic variation [1]; environmental variation [1] [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Which feature of marram grass reduces water loss?
options: Stomata on the upper surface of floating leaves
Large air spaces in the stem
Leaves that roll up with stomata on the inner surface
items.answer: Leaves that roll up with stomata on the inner surface
items.markingKey: Rolling traps humid air around the stomata.

items.stem: Explain why adaptive features must be inherited to be important in evolution.
items.answer: Only inherited features (alleles) can be passed to offspring, increasing in frequency over generations.

items.stem: Sofia measured the percentage loss in mass of shoots of four plant species, each standing in a test-tube of water covered with oil, over 24 hours in the same conditions. Results table. Plant species: oleander, cactus, water lily, marram grass. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 3.6, 0.7, 11.9, 1.7; trial 2: 2.4, 0.6, 11.9, 1.6; trial 3: 2.5, 0.6, 12.1, 1.7. Explain why a layer of oil was placed on the water in each test-tube.
items.answer: To stop water evaporating from the surface of the water, so all mass lost is from the shoot.

items.stem: A student counted stomata in a field of view of area 0.1 mm² on leaves of oleander and of a bean plant (a mesophyte). Oleander: upper surface 0, lower surface 24. Bean: upper surface 6, lower surface 26. (a) Calculate the number of stomata per mm² on the lower surface of the oleander. (b) Calculate the total stomata per mm² (both surfaces) for each plant. (c) Suggest how the distribution of stomata in oleander is an adaptation to its habitat.
items.answer: (a) 240 per mm² (b) oleander 240; bean 320 per mm² (c) few stomata, mostly on the lower surface (or inside rolled leaves), reducing water loss.
items.markingKey: (a) 24 ÷ 0.1 = 240 [1] (b) 240 [1]; 320 [1] (c) xerophyte adaptation explained [2] [5]

items.stem: Freya measured the percentage loss in mass of shoots of four plant species, each standing in a test-tube of water covered with oil, over 24 hours in the same conditions. Results table. Plant species: oleander, marram grass, bean, water lily. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 2.2, 1.6, 7.7, 11.4; trial 2: 3.2, 1.5, 7.9, 10.7; trial 3: 2.3, 1.5, 7.8, 10.8. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (c) Explain why a layer of oil was placed on the water in each test-tube.
items.answer: (a) Independent: plant species; dependent: percentage loss in mass. (b) Temperature; light intensity. (c) To stop water evaporating from the surface of the water, so all mass lost is from the shoot.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = plant species [1]; dependent variable = percentage loss in mass [1] [2] (b) Any two from: temperature; light intensity; humidity / air movement; time; initial mass or leaf area of the shoot [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "natural selection"?
options: The ability of bacteria to survive treatment with an antibiotic that would normally kill them.
The change in adaptive features of a population over time as a result of natural selection.
The process by which individuals with better adapted features are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
The process, resulting from natural selection, by which populations become more suited to their environment over many generations.
items.answer: The process by which individuals with better adapted features are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
items.markingKey: Natural selection: the process by which individuals with better adapted features are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.

items.stem: Explain why there is a struggle for survival in natural populations.
items.answer: Organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support, so they compete for limited resources such as food, mates and space.

items.stem: Explain why resistance spreads faster in bacteria than adaptations spread in mammals.
items.answer: Bacteria reproduce very quickly (short generation time), so many generations occur in a short time.

items.stem: In a hospital in Doha, the percentage of Staphylococcus infections resistant to an antibiotic rose from 7.6% in 2008 to 25.3% in 2020. (a) Calculate the mean increase per year in percentage points. (b) Suggest two reasons for this increase.
items.answer: (a) 1.48 percentage points per year (b) overuse of antibiotics / not completing courses / use in farming, selecting resistant bacteria.

items.stem: Mohammed placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria, incubated it at 25 °C for 2 days and measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Results table. Concentration of antibiotic / µg/cm³: 0, 5, 10, 20, 40. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 6, 11, 14, 16, 18; trial 2: 6, 12, 14, 16, 18; trial 3: 6, 11, 14, 16, 18. Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: As the concentration of antibiotic increases, the diameter of clear zone increases (from 6 to 18).
items.markingKey: correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: In a population of rabbits, some individuals have thicker fur. During a period of very cold winters, the proportion of rabbits with thicker fur increased over several generations. (a) Explain why the change takes several generations. (b) Compare natural selection with selective breeding.
items.answer: (a) Allele frequencies change only when individuals reproduce; each generation increases the proportion a little. (b) Natural selection: environment chooses, features that aid survival, slow; selective breeding: humans choose features useful to humans, faster.

items.stem: Priya writes in a revision note: "Selective breeding creates new genes." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Selective breeding changes the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles come from mutation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Selective breeding changes the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles come from mutation. [2]

items.stem: A student in Nairobi states: "Selective breeding creates new genes." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Selective breeding changes the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles come from mutation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Selective breeding changes the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles come from mutation. [2]

items.stem: Which feature would a grower whose crops are attacked by rust fungus most want to select for in wheat?
items.answer: Disease resistance
items.markingKey: A grower whose crops are attacked by rust fungus: disease resistance.

items.stem: Describe how selective breeding is carried out and discuss its advantages and disadvantages.
items.answer: Choose parents with desired features; breed; select best offspring; repeat for many generations. Advantages: higher yield, disease resistance, desired features. Disadvantages: reduced variation, inbreeding, susceptibility to disease, animal welfare problems, slow.
items.markingKey: procedure [3]; two advantages [1]; two disadvantages [2] [6]

items.stem: Which factor increases the rate of mutation?
items.answer: Ionising radiation
items.markingKey: Ionising radiation (e.g. X-rays, gamma rays) is a mutagen.

items.stem: Explain why workers using X-ray machines stand behind lead screens.
items.answer: X-rays are ionising radiation, a mutagen; reducing exposure lowers the risk of mutations (and cancer).
items.markingKey: mutagen [1]; less risk of mutation / cancer [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists in Dubai exposed fruit flies to different doses of X-rays and counted the number of mutants per 10 000 offspring. Dose / arbitrary units: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Mutants per 10 000: 5, 15, 26, 36, 46. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the number of mutants between dose 0 and dose 1. (b) Describe the relationship shown. (c) Explain why there are some mutants even at dose 0.
items.answer: (a) 200% (b) as dose increases, the number of mutants increases (roughly in proportion). (c) Mutations happen randomly / spontaneously (or from background radiation).
items.markingKey: (a) (15 − 5) ÷ 5 × 100 [1] = 200% [1] (b) positive correlation [1] (c) spontaneous / background radiation [1] [4]

items.stem: The heights of 45 students at a school in Riyadh were grouped into classes: 140–149 cm: 2; 150–159 cm: 14; 160–169 cm: 17; 170–179 cm: 9; 180–189 cm: 3. (a) State the modal class. (b) Calculate the percentage of students in the class 150–159 cm. (c) Explain whether this shows continuous or discontinuous variation.
items.answer: (a) 160–169 cm (b) 31.1% (c) continuous: a range of values between two extremes (data had to be grouped).

items.stem: Compare continuous and discontinuous variation, giving examples, and describe how mutation produces new alleles.
items.answer: Continuous: range between extremes, many genes + environment, e.g. height, histogram. Discontinuous: distinct categories, genes only, e.g. blood group, bar chart. Mutation: random change in base sequence, rate increased by ionising radiation / chemicals; only source of new alleles.
items.markingKey: continuous described with example [2]; discontinuous described with example [2]; mutation and mutagens [2] [6]

items.stem: Why do water lilies have stomata on the upper surface of their leaves?
options: The lower surface is in contact with water, so gas exchange must happen with the air above
items.answer: The lower surface is in contact with water, so gas exchange must happen with the air above
items.markingKey: Upper stomata allow CO₂ in and O₂ out from the air.

items.stem: Arjun says: "Hydrophytes have a thick waxy cuticle to keep water out." Explain whether Arjun is correct.
items.answer: Hydrophytes have a thin or absent cuticle; water loss is not a problem for them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Hydrophytes have a thin or absent cuticle; water loss is not a problem for them. [2]

items.stem: Noah measured the percentage loss in mass of shoots of four plant species, each standing in a test-tube of water covered with oil, over 24 hours in the same conditions. Results table. Plant species: bean, oleander, water lily, marram grass. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 4.3, 2.2, 10.5, 1.4; trial 2: 7.3, 2.1, 10.7, 1.5; trial 3: 7, 2.1, 10.5, 1.5. Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: The water lily lost the highest percentage of mass and the marram grass the lowest; xerophytes lost much less than other plants.
items.markingKey: correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara measured the percentage loss in mass of shoots of four plant species, each standing in a test-tube of water covered with oil, over 24 hours in the same conditions. Results table. Plant species: water lily, bean, oleander, marram grass. Percentage loss in mass / %, trial 1: 12.5, 8.6, 2.4, 1.7; trial 2: 12.5, 8.3, 2.5, 1.7; trial 3: 12.6, 5.2, 2.4, 1.7. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (c) State the type of graph that should be drawn to display these results and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Trial 3 for bean (5.2 %); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Use percentage change in mass so shoots of different starting masses can be compared. (c) A bar chart, because the independent variable (plant species) is categoric.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 3 for bean identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) Any one from: use percentage change in mass so shoots of different starting masses can be compared; measure the leaf surface area and express the loss per cm²; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the plant species (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (c) bar chart [1]; categoric variable [1] [2]

items.stem: Marram grass grows on coastal sand dunes near Perth. The sand drains quickly and the dunes are exposed to strong, dry winds. In dry weather its leaves roll up, with the stomata on the inner surface among many hairs. (a) State the term for a plant adapted to dry conditions. (b) Explain how rolling of the leaves reduces water loss. (c) Suggest the advantage of very long roots to marram grass.
items.answer: (a) Xerophyte. (b) Moist air is trapped inside the roll, so the water vapour concentration gradient is reduced and less water diffuses out of the stomata; less surface exposed to wind. (c) They reach water deep in the sand and anchor the plant in shifting sand.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) humid air trapped [1]; smaller diffusion gradient [1]; less exposure to wind [1] [3] (c) [2]

items.stem: State why antibiotics are not used to treat viral diseases.
items.answer: Antibiotics do not affect viruses (they target bacterial structures).

items.stem: A student in Cape Town states: "Natural selection produces the mutations an organism needs." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Mutations are random; natural selection only changes how often existing alleles are passed on.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Mutations are random; natural selection only changes how often existing alleles are passed on. [2]

items.stem: Felix says: "Bacteria become resistant because they get used to the antibiotic." Explain whether Felix is correct.
items.answer: Resistance comes from a random mutation; the antibiotic only selects resistant bacteria, which survive and reproduce.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Resistance comes from a random mutation; the antibiotic only selects resistant bacteria, which survive and reproduce. [2]

items.stem: In a hospital in Dhaka, the percentage of Staphylococcus infections resistant to an antibiotic rose from 3.7% in 2010 to 13.0% in 2018. (a) Calculate the mean increase per year in percentage points. (b) Suggest two reasons for this increase.
items.answer: (a) 1.16 percentage points per year (b) overuse of antibiotics / not completing courses / use in farming, selecting resistant bacteria.

items.stem: Felix placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria, incubated it at 25 °C for 2 days and measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Results table. Concentration of antibiotic / µg/cm³: 0, 5, 10, 20, 40. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 6, 12, 15, 16, 18; trial 2: 6, 11, 15, 16, 18; trial 3: 6, 12, 14, 17, 19. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: Independent: concentration of antibiotic; dependent: diameter of clear zone.
items.markingKey: independent variable = concentration of antibiotic [1]; dependent variable = diameter of clear zone [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria, incubated it at 25 °C for 2 days and measured the diameter of the clear zone around each disc. Results table. Concentration of antibiotic / µg/cm³: 0, 5, 10, 20, 40. Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 6, 11, 13, 15, 17; trial 2: 6, 11, 13, 15, 17; trial 3: 6, 11, 19, 15, 16. (a) Explain the results. (b) State why the plates were incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C.
items.answer: (a) Antibiotic diffuses out from the disc into the agar and kills bacteria; a higher concentration gives a steeper gradient and reaches killing concentration further from the disc, so the clear zone is wider. (b) To reduce the risk of growing human pathogens.
items.markingKey: (a) diffusion from disc [1]; bacteria killed [1]; higher concentration diffuses further [1] [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Daniel says: "Selective breeding creates new genes." Explain whether Daniel is correct.
items.answer: Selective breeding changes the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles come from mutation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Selective breeding changes the frequency of existing alleles; new alleles come from mutation. [2]

items.stem: A student in Dubai states: "Selective breeding gives the same result as genetic modification." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Selective breeding uses existing variation within a species over many generations; GM transfers specific genes, even between species.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Selective breeding uses existing variation within a species over many generations; GM transfers specific genes, even between species. [2]

items.stem: Which feature would a florist most want to select for in roses?
items.answer: Large, scented flowers
items.markingKey: A florist: large, scented flowers.

items.stem: Over 50 years, breeders in Doha have produced varieties of rice with much greater grain yield than wild types. Some of these varieties are now very similar to each other genetically. (a) Explain one disadvantage of the varieties being genetically similar. (b) Suggest why breeders keep some wild-type individuals or seeds. (c) State two differences between selective breeding and natural selection.
items.answer: (a) Reduced genetic variation means a new disease or environmental change could affect all of them; alleles for resistance may have been lost. (b) They act as a store of alleles (genetic variation) that may be needed in future, e.g. for disease resistance. (c) Humans choose vs environment; features useful to humans vs features aiding survival; faster vs slower.
